newsitem.title: UK: Dust could have warmed, not cooled, Earth - report.
newsitem.headline: Dust could have warmed, not cooled, Earth - report.

text.p: Dust is widely blamed for blocking out the sun and helping worsen some of the Earth's ice ages, but it could also have acted at times to warm up the planet, climatologists said on Wednesday.

Computer simulations show that dust from desert sandstorms could act as a cozy blanket, holding heat to the surface, Jonathan Overpeck, an expert in ancient climate history at the University of Colorado, and his colleagues said.
Their findings could help scientists understand the complex processes that affect global warming today.
Writing in the scientific journal Nature, Overpeck said such dust-induced warming could have helped break up glaciers.

"Here we present a different view based on three-dimensional climate simulations, which suggest that high glacial dust loading may have caused significant, episodic regional warming of over five degrees C (nine degrees F) downwind of major Asian and ice-margin dust sources," they wrote.
Some of the changes are known as Heinrich events, in which flotillas of icebergs were dumped into the oceans from ice sheets covering Europe and North America.
These in turn affected climate more as the ice melted, cooling the water and changing currents.
The warming also caused changes in air circulation patterns, with warm air being pulled from oceans and the south.

"Our results point to dust aerosols as a potential source of episodic warming during the last glacial period, and suggest that this warming might be the trigger mechanism needed to account for previously unexplained major abrupt climate events," Overpeck wrote.
